findings: Split the pipeline into two phases with different SLAs: a synchronous 'accept' path that durably persists the order and flips status to processing within the 5s budget, and an asynchronous 'fulfill' path that talks to warehouse/shipping systems with no tight latency bound — this decouples the customer-facing SLA from the slow, failure-prone external call.

Use the order database write itself (not the queue) as the durable source of truth and point of no return: the API handler inserts the order row (status=received) and only then returns success to the customer, so no order can be lost even if everything downstream of that write fails.

Apply the transactional outbox pattern for enqueueing the fulfillment event: write the order row and an outbox/event row in the same DB transaction, then a separate relay publishes to the queue — this avoids the dual-write problem where a DB write succeeds but the queue publish fails (or vice versa), which is a classic source of lost or duplicate events.

Put a durable, horizontally-scalable log/queue (Kafka, Kinesis, or SQS) between ingestion and fulfillment specifically to absorb the 50x Black Friday burst: producers (API writes) are decoupled from consumer (fulfillment worker) throughput, so a traffic spike becomes queue depth/latency rather than dropped requests or overloaded downstream systems.

Autoscale a pool of stateless fulfillment workers on queue depth/consumer lag so the burst is absorbed by adding consumers rather than by the warehouse/shipping integration having to handle 50x instantaneous load.

Guarantee 'never fulfilled twice' via idempotency keyed on order ID rather than via exactly-once delivery: since queues realistically offer at-least-once delivery, the fulfillment worker must do a conditional/compare-and-swap update (e.g. UPDATE ... WHERE status='processing' SET status='fulfilling') so a redelivered or duplicate message is a safe no-op.

Model order state as an explicit persisted state machine (received -> processing -> fulfilling -> fulfilled / failed) so status transitions are auditable, resumable after a crash, and queryable by the customer-facing UI without depending on queue internals.

Handle transient failures in the warehouse/shipping call with retry + exponential backoff at the worker level, and a dead-letter queue plus alerting for orders that exhaust retries, so failures degrade to 'needs manual attention' rather than silent loss or a stuck customer order.

Use a visibility-timeout/lease-based consumption model (as in SQS/Kafka consumer groups) so that a worker crashing mid-fulfillment causes the message to become available again rather than being lost, while the idempotent conditional-update guard prevents that redelivery from causing double fulfillment.

Partition the queue/log by order ID (or a derived key) where per-order ordering matters, while allowing full parallelism across different orders, so the burst can be spread across many partitions/consumers without violating any single order's event ordering.

Separate the customer-visible 'processing' status update from actual fulfillment completion in the API/UI layer, so the 5-second UX guarantee is met by a fast DB write and status flag rather than by waiting on the warehouse/shipping integration.

Favor managed, horizontally-scalable infrastructure (managed queue + autoscaling compute) over a custom-built broker or in-memory queue, since building durable at-least-once delivery, replay, and backpressure handling from scratch is exactly the kind of reliability engineering that's error-prone and unnecessary to reinvent.

Add monitoring/alerting on queue depth, consumer lag, and DLQ size so operators get early warning of a backlog forming during the spike, before it threatens either the 5-second SLA or the no-lost-order guarantee.

Explicitly reject a design where the API call synchronously invokes the warehouse/shipping system, because that ties customer-facing latency and burst capacity directly to a slow, transient-failure-prone external dependency — the queue-based decoupling is the core answer to the bursty-traffic constraint.
